paragraphs: Imitation learning trains agents from expert demonstrations, but obtaining enough demonstrations to cover deployment situations can be expensive. This paper asks whether learning useful internal representations through additional training objectives can reduce that burden. The motivation comes from successes in other areas, including vision and language, where representation learning has helped make better use of task-specific data.

The authors build a modular framework for assembling representation learning algorithms and use it to evaluate imitation learning across several environment suites. Their comparison includes a carefully tuned baseline that uses image augmentations. This makes the question concrete: do the additional representation learning methods offer value beyond that baseline?

In the evaluated settings, existing image-based representation learning algorithms provide limited additional benefit. The authors investigate differences between imitation learning and settings such as image classification to understand this result. Their findings qualify the expectation that benefits transfer automatically between tasks. They also release documented, reusable code for reproducing the study and constructing new algorithms.
neurips-2021-an-empirical-investigation-.tldr: Across the evaluated imitation learning settings, existing representation learning methods add limited value beyond a well-tuned baseline with image augmentations.

paragraphs: Person re-identification models need to remain useful when their input images are corrupted, particularly in safety-critical applications. Evaluations on clean images alone do not establish that robustness. This paper introduces five benchmarks that make corrupted-image performance an explicit evaluation target, covering both single-modality and cross-modality person re-identification.

The authors reproduce and assess 21 recent methods. In their study, transformer-based models handle corruptions better than convolutional models. They also find that raising the probability of random erasing, a commonly used training augmentation, hurts corruption robustness. That observation matters because increasing an augmentation does not necessarily improve the particular kind of robustness being tested.

The experiments additionally associate greater corruption robustness with better generalization across datasets. Drawing on these observations, the authors propose a baseline that improves robustness against diverse corruptions in both modality settings. The contribution combines a shared evaluation resource with empirical guidance about model and training choices; the reported comparisons concern the methods and conditions examined in the study.
neurips-2021-benchmarks-for-corruption-i.tldr: Five benchmarks reveal how person re-identification methods respond to image corruption and support a baseline with improved robustness.

paragraphs: Weather and climate simulations spend substantial computation on physical processes, including atmospheric radiative transfer. Neural networks offer a way to approximate these expensive calculations with faster predictions. However, comparing such replacements has been difficult because prior studies lacked a comprehensive shared dataset and standardized benchmarking practices.

ClimART addresses that evaluation gap with more than 10 million samples derived from the Canadian Earth System Model. The data span present, pre-industrial, and future climate conditions. This scope makes the benchmark relevant to evaluating approximations across different climate conditions, alongside the more basic question of how accurately a network reproduces the target calculations.

The benchmark includes multiple tests outside the training distribution and highlights the need to account for domain physics and the trade-off between accuracy and prediction speed. The authors also introduce baselines whose results expose shortcomings in datasets and architectures used previously. The contribution is a resource for assessing radiative-transfer emulators, with computational efficiency and generalization treated as central parts of the problem.
neurips-2021-climart-a-benchmark-dataset.tldr: ClimART provides over 10 million climate-model samples for comparing the accuracy, speed, and generalization of atmospheric radiative-transfer emulators.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning benchmarks strongly shape which capabilities researchers can study. Widely used environments do not always isolate particular abilities, while specialized environments can be difficult to expand once a method moves beyond a small demonstration. MiniHack addresses this problem by providing a framework for creating and extending custom reinforcement learning environments.

The framework draws on the entities and dynamics of NetHack, a rich grid-based game. Researchers can construct environments ranging from small rooms to complex worlds generated procedurally. They can specify tasks through a human-readable description language or a simple Python interface, making environment design a direct part of the experimental workflow.

MiniHack also supplies tasks and baselines and can wrap existing benchmarks to add complexity. Its value lies in supporting a progression from focused tests of capabilities toward richer settings within one framework. The paper presents infrastructure for research on problems such as exploration, transfer, environment design, and language-assisted learning, rather than claiming that the framework itself solves those problems.
neurips-2021-minihack-the-planet-a-sandb.tldr: MiniHack lets researchers build and extend reinforcement learning environments from simple rooms to complex procedurally generated worlds.

paragraphs: Forecasting methods increasingly learn across collections of time series instead of treating every series independently. Evaluating these global and multivariate approaches requires datasets containing suitable groups of series, with enough variety to test performance across different conditions. This paper addresses the lack of a comprehensive archive designed to support those comparisons.

The archive brings together 25 publicly available datasets from different domains. They vary in observation frequency, sequence length, and whether values are missing. These differences give researchers multiple forecasting conditions to work with. The authors also analyze dataset features to characterize which collections resemble one another and which capture different kinds of forecasting problems.

Alongside the data, the paper reports results for standard forecasting baselines using ten error metrics across the archive. Those results provide reference points for evaluating new methods. The contribution is therefore both a dataset collection and a benchmarking foundation: researchers can compare algorithms across varied data and scoring measures rather than relying on an isolated dataset.
neurips-2021-monash-time-series-forecast.tldr: The Monash archive combines 25 diverse time-series datasets with feature analyses and baseline results to support broader forecasting comparisons.

paragraphs: The Multilingual Spoken Words Corpus provides audio examples for keyword spotting and spoken-term search across 50 languages collectively spoken by more than five billion people. It contains over 340,000 keywords and 23.4 million one-second examples, totaling more than 6,000 hours. The resource supports both academic research and commercial applications under a CC-BY 4.0 license.

The authors build the collection from crowdsourced recordings of complete sentences. They apply forced alignment to estimate where individual words occur, then extract word-level audio using those timing estimates. Including all alignments makes the timing information part of the released dataset, alongside the extracted examples.

The paper analyzes the collection and introduces methods for identifying potential outliers. It also reports keyword-spotting baseline accuracies and compares models trained on this corpus with models trained on manually recorded keywords. These comparisons help assess the resulting training resource. The contribution combines multilingual scale with a documented construction process and plans for maintenance, updates, and open-source code.
neurips-2021-multilingual-spoken-words-c.tldr: This corpus extracts 23.4 million spoken-word examples in 50 languages from crowdsourced sentence recordings for keyword and speech-search research.

paragraphs: A model's test accuracy depends on the correctness of the labels used to judge it. This paper investigates labeling errors in ten widely used vision, language, and audio test sets. It estimates an average error rate of at least 3.3% across those datasets, including at least 6% in the ImageNet validation set.

The authors use confident learning algorithms to flag suspected errors, then ask crowdsourced human reviewers to validate them. On average, 51% of flagged candidates are confirmed as mislabeled. This distinction matters: an algorithm's suspicion is a starting point for review, rather than automatic evidence that a label is wrong.

The study shows that label corrections and the prevalence of originally mislabeled examples can affect model rankings. On corrected ImageNet labels, ResNet-18 surpasses ResNet-50 when that prevalence increases by 6%; a corresponding 5% increase reverses the VGG-11 versus VGG-19 comparison on CIFAR-10. These conditional findings suggest that smaller models may be more useful in some noisy-data settings and motivate greater care when choosing models from benchmark accuracy.
neurips-2021-pervasive-label-errors-in-t.tldr: Widespread test-label errors can change benchmark conclusions, including which model appears preferable under particular noisy-data conditions.

paragraphs: Comparing reinforcement learning traffic-signal controllers requires shared control problems and implementations. This paper introduces a toolkit that supplies both, combining implementations of leading deep reinforcement learning methods with benchmark problems based on realistic traffic scenarios. It establishes a common setting for comparing existing controllers and evaluating future proposals.

Using the toolkit, the authors examine how algorithms perform when sensing assumptions and intersection layouts vary. Their experiments suggest that earlier methods are not robust to those changes, particularly when intersections depart from simplified layouts. This matters because the information available to a controller and the structure of its signals are part of the control problem itself.

Under more realistic signal layouts and advanced sensing assumptions, a distributed deep-Q learning approach outperforms previously reported leading algorithms in many cases. The result is conditional on those settings and does not establish a universally best controller. Together, the toolkit and comparisons show why traffic-control evaluations should make sensing and layout assumptions explicit when interpreting relative performance.
neurips-2021-reinforcement-learning-benc.tldr: A shared traffic-control toolkit shows that reinforcement learning rankings depend on sensing assumptions and intersection layouts.

paragraphs: A translation test set is useful when it distinguishes between systems in ways that agree with human judgment. This paper develops variance-aware test sets, or VAT, by removing benchmark examples that offer little discrimination between systems. The filtering method is automatic and does not require human labor to construct the resulting sets.

The release contains 70 small test sets covering 35 translation directions from the WMT16 through WMT20 competitions. In experiments across mainstream language pairs and test sets, evaluation on VAT correlates better with human judgments than evaluation on the original WMT benchmarks. The finding concerns the quality of system assessment rather than an improvement to the translation systems themselves.

The authors also examine what makes the retained examples challenging. Their analysis identifies features such as low-frequency words and proper nouns as difficulties for competitive translation systems. These observations offer guidance for future test-set construction: selecting examples that expose meaningful differences can improve evaluation even when the resulting test sets are small.
neurips-2021-variance-aware-machine-tran.tldr: Automatically filtered translation test sets distinguish systems more effectively and correlate better with human judgments in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics from images is difficult because observations do not directly reveal a system's underlying state. Some machine learning approaches address this by building assumptions from classical mechanics into their models. This paper examines whether those physical priors deliver practical improvements when models must infer dynamics from visual observations.

The authors introduce 17 datasets based on physical systems with a wide range of dynamics. They compare major classes of physically inspired methods with strong standard baselines. This design separates two questions: whether physical assumptions produce useful properties in the learned internal representation, and whether those properties translate into better performance.

The experiments find that physically informed models can often learn latent spaces with desirable properties, yet do not significantly improve on standard techniques in the comparison. At the same time, continuous and time-reversible dynamics benefit models across all classes examined. The results therefore distinguish particular useful modeling choices from a broader expectation that incorporating physical priors will automatically improve learning.
neurips-2021-which-priors-matter-benchma.tldr: Physical priors do not significantly beat standard methods in this benchmark, although continuous and time-reversible dynamics benefit all model classes examined.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to reduce labeling effort by choosing which training examples receive labels. Although neural-network approaches have shown empirical success, rigorous guarantees about the number of labels they require have been harder to establish. This paper studies the problem through nonparametric classification and provides near-optimal label-complexity guarantees for deep active learning.

Under standard low-noise conditions, the authors show that neural-network active learning can reach the minimax label complexity up to a disagreement coefficient and logarithmic factors. This characterizes performance relative to a worst-case statistical benchmark while preserving the factors and assumptions that qualify the result.

The paper also develops an efficient algorithm with an abstention option: it can decline to make a prediction. With that option, it obtains label complexity polynomial in the logarithm of inverse target error, without low-noise assumptions. Finally, the analysis extends beyond Sobolev and Hölder spaces to Radon BV² spaces associated with neural networks. These results connect neural active learning to statistical guarantees under explicitly different prediction settings.
neurips-2022-active-learning-with-neural.tldr: Nonparametric analysis yields near-optimal neural active-learning label guarantees under low noise and stronger label savings when abstention is allowed.

paragraphs: Emphatic reinforcement learning changes how strongly different learning updates are weighted. Its emphasis depends on an interest function that assigns importance to states. Most approaches use the same interest everywhere unless domain knowledge supports a manually designed alternative. This paper investigates learning that interest function automatically as the agent trains.

The proposed methods allow interest to vary across both states and training iterations. They use meta-gradients to discover an interest function online with the aim of accelerating learning. This makes the allocation of learning emphasis itself adjustable, rather than fixing every state's importance before the learning process begins.

Across a wide range of evaluated environments, adapting interest produces significant gains. Qualitative analysis shows that learned interest highlights particularly important states, including bottlenecks. Such emphasis can be especially useful in transfer learning, according to the study. The findings support adaptive state importance as a useful component of emphatic methods, with the empirical gains tied to the environments and learning settings examined.
neurips-2022-adaptive-interest-for-empha.tldr: Learning which states deserve greater emphasis improves emphatic reinforcement learning across the evaluated environments.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference can become expensive when it must use an entire dataset. A coreset replaces that dataset with a small weighted selection of observations, producing an approximate posterior on which inference is cheaper. Existing construction methods can themselves be slow or require users to supply an inexpensive approximation to the full posterior.

This paper proposes a two-stage construction method. It first selects observations uniformly at random, then adjusts their weights using a new quasi-Newton optimization method. The resulting approach is described as simple to implement and usable as a black box, without requiring the user to design a separate low-cost posterior approximation.

The authors provide a general high-probability bound on the KL divergence of the resulting coreset posterior, giving a probabilistic characterization of approximation quality. Experiments show better coresets than alternatives with comparable construction times, alongside substantially lower storage requirements and less user input. The approach therefore addresses the cost of constructing the approximation as well as the cost of subsequently using it.
neurips-2022-fast-bayesian-coresets-via-.tldr: Random subsampling followed by quasi-Newton weight optimization produces efficient Bayesian coresets with a high-probability approximation bound.

paragraphs: In federated recommender and language systems, a large embedding layer may contain many features, while each client uses only a small subset. Some features occur across many clients and others across few. This paper identifies that imbalance as a source of slow optimization when client updates are combined through standard federated averaging.

Parameters associated with common, or hot, features receive updates more quickly than parameters associated with rare, or cold, features. The proposed method, FedSubAvg, uses the number of clients associated with each feature to correct how submodel updates are aggregated. Its aggregation therefore accounts explicitly for differences in feature participation.

The authors prove that variation in feature heat makes the global objective ill-conditioned and explain FedSubAvg as a diagonal preconditioner that addresses this imbalance. They also analyze its convergence rate to stationary points. Evaluations on public and industrial datasets show significant improvements over FedAvg and its variants, linking the optimization analysis to practical performance in the studied sparse-model settings.
neurips-2022-federated-submodel-optimiza.tldr: FedSubAvg corrects federated update aggregation for unequal feature participation, improving optimization in the evaluated sparse-model tasks.

paragraphs: Rank estimation involves predicting an ordered value, where both relative position and the size of a difference matter. This paper proposes geometric order learning, or GOL, to represent those relationships directly in an embedding space. The goal is to make the geometry of learned representations reflect the ranks being predicted.

Two constraints shape that space. An order constraint arranges objects according to their ranks, while a metric constraint makes distances reflect rank differences. Direction and distance thus serve related but distinct purposes. Once the representation is learned, the method estimates a new object's rank through a simple k-nearest-neighbor search in that space.

The authors also introduce the discriminative ratio for ranking, a measure intended to assess embedding quality for this task. Experiments on facial age estimation, historical color image classification, and aesthetic score regression demonstrate effective embeddings and strong rank-estimation performance. The approach makes representation design central: a simple neighbor-based prediction method becomes useful because training explicitly organizes the space around ordered relationships.
neurips-2022-geometric-order-learning-fo.tldr: GOL learns embeddings whose directions and distances encode rank relationships, enabling effective rank prediction with nearest-neighbor search.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through binary spikes, a mechanism that can be highly energy efficient on neuromorphic hardware because it avoids multiplications. However, converting signals into zero-or-one spikes loses information and can reduce accuracy. This paper targets that training problem with an information-maximization objective called IM-Loss.

IM-Loss aims to increase information flow and improve the network's expressive capacity. It also performs part of the role of normalization without adding inference-time operations such as bias or scaling. This matters because improving the trained model need not introduce those additional operations when the model is deployed.

The paper pairs the loss with Evolutionary Surrogate Gradients, a differentiable estimate of spike activity whose surrogate gradients evolve automatically during training. The method is designed to provide sufficient updates early and accurate gradients later, supporting convergence and task performance. Experiments on both static non-spiking datasets and neuromorphic datasets report improvements over the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution combines an information-preserving objective with an adaptive mechanism for training through spike activity.
neurips-2022-im-loss-information-maximiz.tldr: IM-Loss and evolving surrogate gradients improve spiking-network training and outperform the compared methods on static and neuromorphic datasets.

paragraphs: Searching for graph neural network architectures can require substantial computation, and inconsistent experimental settings make results difficult to compare or reproduce. NAS-Bench-Graph addresses both problems by defining a shared search space and evaluation protocol. Its search space contains 26,206 distinct graph neural network architectures.

The authors train and evaluate every architecture on nine graph datasets. They record training, validation, and test performance at each epoch, together with information such as latency and parameter count. Researchers can then obtain the recorded performance through table lookup rather than repeatedly training the same candidate architectures.

This changes the cost of evaluating search methods within the benchmark: the expensive architecture evaluations have already been performed under a common protocol. The paper also analyzes the benchmark and demonstrates compatibility with graph architecture-search libraries including AutoGL and NNI. Its contribution is a reusable basis for efficient and reproducible comparisons within the supplied architecture space and datasets, making those experiments more accessible to researchers with limited computation.
neurips-2022-nas-bench-graph-benchmarkin.tldr: NAS-Bench-Graph precomputes results for 26,206 graph architectures on nine datasets to make architecture-search comparisons cheaper and reproducible.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions when both rewards and constraints are unknown. The functions can be nonlinear and nonconvex, but are assumed to have bounded norms in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Unlike settings that demand safety at every step, the problem allows individual constraint violations provided their cumulative amount remains small.

The authors use primal-dual optimization to build a framework for algorithm design and analysis. A new sufficient condition connects the framework to multiple exploration strategies, including upper confidence bounds, Thompson sampling, and random exploration. This lets several approaches be studied through a common argument rather than requiring an entirely separate analysis for each.

The framework supports guarantees of sublinear regret together with sublinear, or in some cases zero, cumulative constraint violation. These are qualified guarantees under the framework's conditions, not a requirement that every round satisfy the constraint. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world data show superior performance for the proposed algorithms. The paper also compares two common analytical approaches for constrained bandits and decision processes.
neurips-2022-on-kernelized-multi-armed-b.tldr: A primal-dual framework gives unified reward and cumulative-constraint guarantees for several exploration strategies in kernelized bandits.

paragraphs: Satellite imagery offers abundant unlabeled data, along with structure across time and spectral bands. SatMAE adapts masked-autoencoder pre-training to exploit those properties before supervised training on remote-sensing tasks. The paper investigates how to represent these additional dimensions so that pre-training benefits from information beyond an individual conventional image.

For temporal imagery, the framework adds temporal embeddings and masks image patches independently across time. For multispectral imagery, it groups spectral bands and assigns distinct spectral positional encodings to those groups. The authors find that this band-grouping representation is beneficial, making spectral identity an explicit part of the model's input representation.

The reported results improve on previous leading techniques in both supervised benchmark performance and transfer to downstream tasks. Improvements reach up to 7% on supervised benchmarks and up to 14% for land-cover classification, with gains also reported for semantic segmentation. Those figures describe reported upper improvements rather than uniform gains. The findings support pre-training choices tailored to the temporal and spectral organization of satellite data.
neurips-2022-satmae-pre-training-transfo.tldr: SatMAE incorporates temporal and spectral structure into masked-autoencoder pre-training, improving performance and transfer on evaluated satellite-imagery tasks.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained model often involves updating all its parameters or training only its final linear layer. The former is expensive, while the latter can sacrifice accuracy. This paper proposes SSF, a method that learns how to scale and shift the model's deep features using a small set of trainable parameters.

The learned adjustments can be merged into the original model weights through reparameterization for inference. Consequently, the extra learnable parameters are needed during training without remaining as additional inference-time components. This gives the method an efficiency advantage that extends beyond reducing the number of parameters being optimized.

With about 0.3 million tuned parameters, SSF reports 90.72% versus 88.54% top-1 accuracy for full fine-tuning on FGVC, and 73.10% versus 65.57% on VTAB-1k. It also outperforms other parameter-efficient approaches with fewer tunable parameters in the reported comparisons. Experiments across convolutional networks, transformers, and MLPs, covering 26 classification datasets and three robustness or distribution-shift datasets, provide evidence for the method across varied evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-scaling-shifting-your-featu.tldr: SSF adapts pretrained models through learned feature scales and shifts that can be merged into model weights, achieving strong accuracy with few tuned parameters.

paragraphs: Second Thoughts treats alignment with human values as a process of revising text. The method models a chain of edits connecting text that is unaligned with those values to text that is aligned. This makes the sequence of changes part of what the language model learns, giving the approach an explicit revision structure.

Training combines language-model fine-tuning with further refinement through reinforcement learning. The learned editing steps also provide something people can inspect and correct interactively. Their value is therefore twofold: they support producing revised text and offer a more interpretable route through the changes that lead to it.

The authors report superior performance on three value-alignment benchmarks and strong transfer in few-shot scenarios, where only a small number of examples are available. Extensive human evaluations further support the method's effectiveness. These findings provide evidence for learning alignment through edit sequences in the evaluated settings. The reported transfer result also suggests that the learned revision process can help when examples for a new alignment setting are scarce.
neurips-2022-second-thoughts-are-best-le.tldr: Second Thoughts learns edit sequences that improve value alignment while making revisions easier to interpret and correct interactively.

paragraphs: Unsupervised learning can aim to uncover interacting hidden causes, beyond fitting a data distribution or generating samples. When several hidden variables can explain the same observation, observing it can make those variables dependent. This phenomenon, called explaining away, creates a challenge for inference methods that do not represent those dependencies.

The paper extends amortized variational inference with structured factors involving multiple variables. These factors capture observation-induced dependencies and allow complex observations to depend on several nodes in a probabilistic graph. The authors show that appropriately parameterized factors can be combined efficiently with variational message passing across rich graphical structures.

They instantiate the framework in nonlinear Gaussian Process Factor Analysis and evaluate it on synthetic data with known generating processes. They also fit the model to high-dimensional hippocampal neural-spike recordings from freely moving rodents. The recovered latent signals correlate with behavioral covariates. This demonstrates the framework's ability to identify behavior-related hidden signals in that application, while the reported correlations do not by themselves establish causal relationships.
neurips-2022-structured-recognition-for-.tldr: Structured variational inference captures dependencies between hidden causes and recovers behavior-correlated latent signals from hippocampal recordings.

paragraphs: Meta-learning can give agents useful tendencies for learning new tasks, but those tendencies need not resemble human strategies. This paper investigates whether additional training on language and program representations can guide agents toward more human-like inductive biases. The central question is which kinds of task descriptions provide that guidance.

The authors co-train agents to predict representations derived from natural-language task descriptions and programs induced to generate the tasks. Human-written descriptions and programs with newly learned primitives can express abstract concepts that shorten descriptions. Those representations supply information about how tasks can be organized through reusable ideas.

Downstream meta-reinforcement learning agents show more human-like behavior with these representations than with less abstract controls: synthetic language descriptions and program induction without learned primitives. The comparison suggests that abstraction is an important contributor to the observed behavior. It does not establish that language or programs automatically produce human-like learning; the supported finding concerns the particular representations and controls examined, and the abstract concepts they make available during co-training.
neurips-2022-using-natural-language-and-.tldr: Co-training on human language and programs with learned abstractions produces more human-like meta-learning behavior than less abstract controls.

paragraphs: Explaining an image classifier often means identifying which image regions contribute to a particular class score. Many methods use internal activations and gradients or repeatedly modify the input. This paper instead trains a separate network to predict explanations for an already pretrained black-box classifier.

The second network, called the Explainer, produces masks that retain classifier-relevant image regions and hide the rest. Its target classifier is called the Explanandum. The approach can directly generate distinct masks for different classes in one forward pass, making explanation generation efficient after the Explainer has been trained.

The authors report masks with sharper, more precise boundaries than saliency maps from other methods. Evaluations on PASCAL VOC-2007 and Microsoft COCO-2014 show both visual and quantitative improvements over established approaches. The contribution combines a learned explanation mechanism with class-specific outputs: the same image can receive different masks depending on the class being explained. The evidence supports the quality and inference efficiency of these attributions in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2022-what-you-see-is-what-you-cl.tldr: A separately trained Explainer generates sharp, class-specific image masks in one forward pass for a pretrained black-box classifier.

paragraphs: Video question answering usually needs multimodal training data, but manually writing questions and answers for videos is laborious. FrozenBiLM targets a zero-shot setting without manually annotated visual question-answer pairs. It builds on a frozen bidirectional language model and presents it as a stronger, cheaper alternative to approaches using frozen autoregressive language models.

Lightweight trainable modules connect visual inputs to the language model. These modules are trained on multimodal data scraped from the web while the language model remains frozen. At inference time, answering a question becomes a masked-language-modeling task: the answer occupies a masked text position that the model predicts using the supplied inputs.

The approach significantly outperforms the reported zero-shot state of the art across a variety of video-question-answering datasets. It also performs competitively in few-shot and fully supervised settings. The result shows that a frozen bidirectional model can support this multimodal task through lightweight adaptation. Zero-shot here concerns the absence of manually annotated visual question-answer training pairs, while multimodal training of the connecting modules still occurs.
neurips-2022-zero-shot-video-question-an.tldr: FrozenBiLM connects videos to a frozen bidirectional language model and answers questions through masked prediction, improving reported zero-shot VideoQA performance.
